purpose: This medicine is used to treat serious bacterial infections in the abdomen and urinary tract caused by bacteria that are resistant to most other antibiotics. It is especially helpful for infections caused by tough, hard-to-treat bacteria called gram-negative bacteria. Doctors use it when other antibiotics have not worked or are unlikely to work.
how_it_works: Aztreonam is an antibiotic that works by stopping bacteria from building their protective outer wall, which kills the bacteria. The problem is that some bacteria produce enzymes that break down aztreonam before it can do its job. That is where avibactam comes in — it blocks those enzymes so aztreonam can keep working effectively against even resistant bacteria.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, headache, increased liver enzyme levels in blood tests, rash, and low potassium levels. Some people may also notice injection site reactions like redness or swelling where the IV is placed.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have a penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, as rare cross-reactions can occur. This medication can cause a serious gut infection called C. difficile — contact your doctor if you develop severe or persistent diarrhea. It may also affect your liver, so regular blood tests may be needed. Always tell your doctor about all your medications and any kidney problems, as the dose may need adjustment.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given through an IV (into a vein) in the hospital, usually over about 3 hours. The typical adult dose is given every 6 hours for 5 to 14 days depending on the type and severity of infection. Your doctor or nurse will handle the exact dose, especially if you have kidney problems.
